title: Ready to Debate Your Side? Bring It to DeHub.
html:
DeHub is not here to tell you what to think. It is here to give you the tools to argue with people who think differently — live, on the record, and without an algorithm quietly deciding which side gets heard.

Israel and Palestine. Abortion. Gun rights. Immigration. Religion. AI and jobs. Free speech. Climate policy.

Pick the issue you actually hold a position on. Now make your case.

The problem is not that people disagree

Disagreement is the point of a public square. The problem is what the big platforms did to it.

Every mainstream feed is ranked by one thing: how long it can keep you scrolling. Argument is extremely good at that, so the systems learned to promote the worst version of every debate — the clip with no context, the quote stripped of its paragraph, the reply that dunks instead of answers. The strongest case for a position rarely travels. The most infuriating one always does.

Then the second layer lands. A topic gets flagged as sensitive, and reach quietly drops for everyone discussing it — the careful and the reckless alike. Nobody tells you. You just post into a room that has been emptied without notice.

The result is a public square that produces heat, no light, and a permanent suspicion that the scales were tipped. People end up shouting past each other and then arguing about whether they were allowed to shout at all.

What a real debate needs

Strip it back and a genuine debate needs four things that social platforms stopped providing:

  • Both sides have to be present. An argument you win because the other side was throttled is not an argument you won.
  • The format has to allow depth. You cannot defend a position on foreign policy in a caption.
  • Distribution has to be honest. If a post is underperforming, it should be because people did not find it convincing — not because a classifier downgraded the topic.
  • Effort has to beat outrage. If the reward for a thoughtful, well-sourced case is less than the reward for a cheap insult, you will get insults.

DeHub is built on decentralised infrastructure specifically so the first three are not somebody's internal policy decision. And it has a rewards layer that works on the fourth.

Where the debate actually happens

Stages — argue live, out loud

Stages are DeHub's live audio rooms. This is the closest thing on the platform to an actual debate hall: a host, invited speakers, and a listening audience who can be brought up to challenge a point.

The format does something text cannot. It is very hard to strawman someone who is in the room and gets to answer thirty seconds later. It is very hard to hide behind a slogan when a stranger can ask you what you actually mean by it. Positions get tested in real time, and listeners hear both people at full strength rather than one person's screenshot of the other.

Run a room on a motion. Invite someone who will disagree with you. Let the audience decide.

Posts, video and long-form — make the full case

Not everything belongs in a live room. Some arguments need to be written down, sourced and left standing so people can come back to them.

DeHub posts carry video, audio and long-form text, so you can publish the twenty-minute breakdown, the annotated document, the explainer that shows why the obvious answer is wrong. It stays on your profile as a reference you can point people to instead of retyping the same argument every week.

Comments — the rebuttal lives with the claim

Threaded comments and reactions sit directly under the argument, not in a separate quote-post ecosystem where each side talks only to its own audience. If you are wrong about a fact, the correction is attached to the thing you said. That is uncomfortable, and it is exactly how it should work.

Polls — find out what the room actually thinks

Attach a poll and get a real read instead of guessing from the loudest replies. Ask before the debate and after it. A motion that moves an audience by ten points is a far more interesting result than a thread with a thousand angry quote-tweets.

Communities — a venue, not a bubble

Communities let you set up a standing venue for a topic, with member roles and moderation rights held by people who actually care about the subject. A weekly debate series, a reading group, a room for one policy area. The moderation is yours to run, in the open, rather than delivered from a trust-and-safety team in another country that has never read your thread.

Getting paid for the good version

This is the part that changes behaviour.

On the ad platforms, the incentive is engagement at any cost, and the person farming outrage earns more than the person doing the reading. DeHub inverts that. Creators earn through subscriptions, tips, paid content and up to 90% ad-revenue share, with POVR rewards tied to proof of genuine viewing rather than raw impressions.

So the economics point somewhere different. A long, careful, genuinely persuasive case that people subscribe to and watch all the way through is worth more than a thirty-second dunk that gets skipped. You are not competing to be the most annoying voice in the topic. You are competing to be the one people pay attention to on purpose.

What this is not

A few things worth being straight about, because "free speech platform" is a phrase that has been used to mean a lot of different things.

This is not an invitation to harass people. It is not a loophole for threats, doxxing, or illegal content. DeHub has moderation, content ratings and reporting, and communities run their own rules on top. Decentralised does not mean unaccountable — it means the rules are visible and the referee is not also the house.

It is also not a promise that you will win. If your position cannot survive contact with someone who has thought hard about the other side, that is useful information. Most of us have at least one belief in that category.

Bring it

If you have spent the last few years convinced you were being quietly buried for saying something reasonable — test it here.

If you have an argument you have never been able to make properly in 280 characters — make it here.

If you think the other side is obviously wrong and you have never actually had to defend your own position to a live human who disagrees — especially here.

Open a Stage. Set a motion. Invite someone who will push back. Post the long version. Run the poll before and after.

Think you can defend your side? Bring the debate to DeHub.
